AIXI

Cluster DD.3.2 · AIXI

Exploring the Bayesian optimal policy for history based reinforcement learning.

By David Quarel (Australian National University)

  • PDFviewdownload
  • LaTeXdownload
  • Markdowndownload
  • SlidespresenthandoutLaTeX

What you’ll learn
  • Formalize the agent-environment interaction, value functions, and the Bayes-optimal policy that defines AIXI.
  • Derive the explicit expectimax form of AIXI.
  • Prove on-policy value convergence and that AIXI cannot be fooled in deterministic environments.
  • Prove the self-optimizing property via likelihood-ratio martingales and change of measure.

Much of this material is drawn from (Hutter et al. 2024). The book provides fuller explanations, additional context, and proofs omitted here.

Difficulty ratings. Each subproblem is tagged with a rating in square brackets using Knuth's scale (Knuth 1973): roughly, [00] trivial, [10] 15–minute pencil-and-paper, [20] 1–2 hours, [30] several hours to a day, [40] a significant research result. Intermediate values are possible. See Appendix B for the full scale.

Problems marked (∗) are less interesting/insightful, and while the result may be used later, I would recommend skipping them on a first pass.

Overview

AIXI is the action half of Universal AI: it lifts the Bayesian mixture from Solomonoff induction — learning to predict — to learning to act. Now the agent takes actions that shape what it observes, and AIXI is the Bayes-optimal policy over a universal mixture ξ of environments. It learns to act as well as if it knew the true environment μ. Under the universal choice — M = all lower-semicomputable environments, prior wν​=2−K(ν) — the assumption "μ∈M" again becomes "the universe is computable."

Prerequisites

  • Solomonoff Induction — start there first. The Bayesian mixture, posterior updates, and dominance carry over directly; AIXI reuses them in the action setting.
  • Comfort with discrete probability (conditional distributions, chain rule, expectations).
  • Familiarity with sequential decision-making / reinforcement learning (agents, rewards, discounting, value functions) is useful but not assumed.

Goal and Roadmap

This exercise sheet builds towards three main results:

  • On-policy value convergence (Section 7): the Bayesian mixture ξ learns to predict the value of any fixed policy as well as the true environment μ.
  • AIXI can't be fooled (Section 8): in deterministic environments, the Bayes-optimal agent is guaranteed non-zero value whenever optimal value is non-zero.
  • Self-optimizing property (Section 11, advanced stretch goal): the Bayes-optimal policy πξ∗​ learns to act as well as if it knew μ, provided that any learnable policy can achieve this. This is the central theoretical justification for the AIXI agent.

A good target is to complete Section 7 and 8. The self-optimizing property (Sections 9–11) requires substantial additional machinery (supermartingales, change of measure) and is an advanced stretch goal.

Critical path. The three results share a common foundation (Sections 0–4) and then diverge:

In summary:

  • Sections 0–4 establish the Bayesian RL framework: measure algebra, mixture properties, existence of optimal policies, dominance, and linearity.
  • Section 5 derives the explicit expectimax form of AIXI.
  • Sections 6–7 prove on-policy value convergence: Vξπ​ and Vμπ​ become indistinguishable for any fixed π.
  • Section 8 shows AIXI can't be fooled: the Bayes-optimal agent achieves non-zero value whenever optimal value is non-zero (in deterministic environments).
  • Sections 9–11 (advanced stretch goal) prove the self-optimizing property: if any policy can learn to act optimally, πξ∗​ inherits this.

Setup

An agent interacts with an environment in discrete time steps t=1,2,….

Definition 0.1 (Spaces and notation). - A: finite set of actions

  • O: finite set of observations
  • R⊂[0,1]: finite set of rewards
  • E:=O×R: set of percepts; et​=(ot​,rt​)≡ot​rt​
  • Ht:=(A×E)t: set of all histories of length t
  • H∗:=∪t=0∞​Ht: set of all finite histories
  • H∞:=(A×E)∞: set of all infinite histories
  • ΔS: set of all probability distributions over set S
  • [[⋅]]: Iverson bracket: [[P]]=1 if P is true, 0 if false
  • t: current time step; m: finite horizon; 1≤t≤m
  • i,j,k: arbitrary integer indices
  • xy: concatenation
  • ϵ: the empty string/history
  • æi:j​:=ai​ei​ai+1​ei+1​⋯aj​ej​: history segment from time i to j
  • æ<t​:=a1​e1​a2​e2​⋯at−1​et−1​: history up to (but not including) time t

Definition 0.2 (Policy π). A policy π:H→ΔA maps each history to a probability distribution over actions. Given history æ<t​:

  • π(⋅∣æ<t​) is a distribution over A,
  • π(at​∣æ<t​)∈[0,1] is the probability of choosing action at​,
  • the agent samples at​∼π(⋅∣æ<t​).

A policy is deterministic if π(a∣æ<t​)∈{0,1} for all a,æ<t​. We write π(æi:j​):=∏k=ij​π(ak​∣æ<k​).

Definition 0.3 (Environment ν). An environment ν:H×A→ΔE maps each history–action pair to a distribution over percepts. Given history æ<t​ and action at​:

  • ν(⋅∣æ<t​at​) is a distribution over E,
  • ν(et​∣æ<t​at​)∈[0,1] is the probability of percept et​,
  • the environment samples et​∼ν(⋅∣æ<t​at​).

We write ν(æi:j​):=∏k=ij​ν(ek​∣æ<k​ak​). This satisfies the chain rule: ν(æi:j​)=ν(æi:j−1​)⋅ν(ej​∣æi:j−1​aj​) or in the form we will usually use, ν(æ1:t​)=ν(æ<t​)⋅ν(et​∣æ<t​at​). An environment is deterministic if ν(et​∣æ<t​at​)∈{0,1} for all et​,æ<t​,at​ (each percept is produced with certainty). We denote the true (unknown) environment by μ.

Definition 0.4 (Interaction measure νπ). When policy π interacts with environment ν, the joint probability of a history segment æi:j​ given past æ<i​ is

νπ(æi:j​∣æ<i​) := k=i∏j​π(ak​∣æ<k​)ν(ek​∣æ<k​ak​).

0. Properties of Measures

Exercise 0.1 (Factorization) [05]. Show that νπ(æ1:t​)=π(æ1:t​)⋅ν(æ1:t​).

Solution

Expanding the definition: νπ(æ1:t​)=∏k=1t​π(ak​∣æ<k​)ν(ek​∣æ<k​ak​)=π(æ1:t​)k=1∏t​π(ak​∣æ<k​)​​⋅ν(æ1:t​)k=1∏t​ν(ek​∣æ<k​ak​)​​.

Key observation: π(æ1:t​) is the same regardless of the environment. When comparing νπ and μπ, the policy factors cancel.

Exercise 0.2 (Chain rule) [05]. Show that ν(æ1:t​)=ν(æ<t​)⋅ν(et​∣æ<t​at​).

Solution

From the definition ν(æ1:t​)=∏k=1t​ν(ek​∣æ<k​ak​), split off the last factor:

ν(æ1:t​) = k=1∏t−1​ν(ek​∣æ<k​ak​)⋅ν(et​∣æ<t​at​) = ν(æ<t​)⋅ν(et​∣æ<t​at​).

Exercise 0.3 (∗) (Marginalizing percepts) [03]. Show that ∑et​​νπ(at​et​∣æ<t​)=π(at​∣æ<t​).

Solution

From Definition 0.4, the one-step interaction is νπ(at​et​∣æ<t​)=π(at​∣æ<t​)ν(et​∣æ<t​at​). Summing over et​:

et​∑​νπ(at​et​∣æ<t​) = π(at​∣æ<t​)=1et​∑​ν(et​∣æ<t​at​)​​ = π(at​∣æ<t​).

Interpretation: after summing out the environment's response, only the agent's action probability remains.

Exercise 0.4 (∗) (Deterministic interaction measure) [05]. Let π be a deterministic policy, i.e. at each history æ<k​ there is a unique action ak∗​ with π(ak∗​∣æ<k​)=1. Show that, provided æi:j​ is consistent with π (i.e. ak​=ak∗​ for every k∈{i,…,j}):

νπ(æi:j​∣æ<i​) = ν(æi:j​∣æ<i​),

i.e. on π-consistent futures the interaction measure reduces to the environment measure: every policy factor is 1.

Solution

Since π is deterministic, π(ak​∣æ<k​)=[[ak​=ak∗​]]. By hypothesis æi:j​ is π-consistent, so every such bracket equals 1. From Definition 0.4:

νπ(æi:j​∣æ<i​)  ​= k=i∏j​=1π(ak​∣æ<k​)​​ν(ek​∣æ<k​ak​)= k=i∏j​ν(ek​∣æ<k​ak​) = ν(æi:j​∣æ<i​),​

where the last equality is the natural segment extension of ν(æ1:t​):=∏k=1t​ν(ek​∣æ<k​ak​).

Exercise 0.5 [05]. (General chain rule for νπ) Show that for any p≤q≤r:

νπ(æp:r​∣æ<p​) = νπ(æp:q​∣æ<p​)⋅νπ(æq+1:r​∣æ<p​æp:q​).
Solution

Split the defining product νπ(æp:r​∣æ<p​)=∏k=pr​π(ak​∣æ<k​)ν(ek​∣æ<k​ak​) at index q:

​νπ(æp:r​∣æ<p​) = k=p∏r​π(ak​∣æ<k​)ν(ek​∣æ<k​ak​)= νπ(æp:q​∣æ<p​)k=p∏q​π(ak​∣æ<k​)ν(ek​∣æ<k​ak​)​​⋅νπ(æq+1:r​∣æ<p​æp:q​)k=q+1∏r​π(ak​∣æ<k​)ν(ek​∣æ<k​ak​)​​,​

identifying each block as a conditional via the same expansion: the past for step k≥q+1 is the given history æ<p​ extended by the first chunk æp:q​.

Note: for a deterministic policy, Exercise 0.4 simplifies this further: each factor π(ak​∣æ<k​)ν(ek​∣æ<k​ak​) becomes just ν(ek​∣æ<k​ak∗​).

The Bayesian Mixture and Value Function

Definition 0.1 (Model class, prior, and Bayesian mixture ξ). Let M={ν1​,ν2​,…} be a countable class of environments with prior weights wν​>0 satisfying ∑ν∈M​wν​≤1. We assume μ∈M.

The Bayesian mixture ξ is defined as

ξ(æ1:t​):=ν∈M∑​wν​ν(æ1:t​) and ξ(et​∣æ<t​at​):=ξ(æ1:t​)/ξ(æ<t​).

One can show that the one-step predictive distribution can be written as

ξ(et​∣æ<t​at​) = ν∈M∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)ν(et​∣æ<t​at​),

where the posterior weight is

w(ν∣æ<t​) := wν​ξ(æ<t​)ν(æ<t​)​,w(ν∣ϵ):=wν​.

See Appendix A for a worked example.

Definition 0.2 (Expectation Eνπ​). For a function f:H→R of a finite future segment æt:m′​:

Eνπ​[f∣æ<t​] := æt:m​∼νπ(⋅∣æ<t​)E​[f] = æt:m′​∑​νπ(æt:m′​∣æ<t​)f(æt:m′​).

For functions f of the infinite future (like the value function), with a sequence f1​,f2​,…→f, where fm​ depends only on æt:m′​, we define Eνπ​[f∣æ<t​]:=limm→∞​Eνπ​[fm​∣æ<t​].

Definition 0.3 (Discounted return Gt:m​). Fix a discount factor γ∈(0,1), held constant throughout. The discounted return at time step t, up to horizon m, is

Gt:mγ​ := k=t+1∑m​γk−(t+1)rk​ = rt+1​+γrt+2​+⋯+γm−trm​.

Since γ is fixed we drop it and write Gt:m​≡Gt:mγ​. It satisfies the recursion Gt:m​=rt+1​+γGt+1:m​, with Gm−1:m​=rm​ and Gn:m​=0 for n≥m. The infinite-horizon return is the pointwise limit

G≥t​ ≡ Gt:∞​ := m→∞lim​Gt:m​ = k=t+1∑∞​γk−(t+1)rk​,

with the clean recursion G≥t​=rt+1​+γG≥t+1​ and no boundary cases.

Definition 0.4 (Value function1). The value of policy π in environment ν with horizon m≥t given history æ<t​ is

  ​Vνπ,m​(æ<t​) := (1−γ)Eνπ​[Gt−1:m​∣æ<t​]= (1−γ)æt:m​∑​νπ(æt:m​∣æ<t​)Gt−1:m​= (1−γ)æt:m​∑​νπ(æt:m​∣æ<t​)[k=t∑m​γk−trk​].​

The infinite-horizon value is the pointwise limit Vνπ,∞​(æ<t​):=limm→∞​Vνπ,m​(æ<t​)=(1−γ)Eνπ​[G≥t−1​∣æ<t​]. We write Vνπ​≡Vνπ,∞​ for short.

The optimal value is Vν∗,m​(æ<t​):=supπ​Vνπ,m​(æ<t​) for m∈N∪{∞}, with Vν∗​≡Vν∗,∞​. 2 An optimal policy πν∗​ satisfies Vνπν∗​​=Vν∗​. The Bayes-optimal policy is πξ∗​∈argmaxπ​Vξπ​.

Remark (AIXI). All results in this sheet hold for any countable M and prior weights wν​. AIXI is a special case of the Bayes-optimal policy πξ∗​ for the particular choice M:= the class of all lower-semicomputable chronological semimeasures, and prior wν​:=2−K(ν), where K(ν) is the Kolmogorov complexity of ν: the length of the shortest program that computes ν. The resulting agent is written πξU​∗​, or simply AIξ.

Why this M? By including every computable environment, the assumption μ∈M reduces to "the universe is computable": as weak an assumption as one can make.

Why this prior? The prior 2−K(ν) is dominant: for any other computable prior wν′​, there exists a constant c>0 such that 2−K(ν)≥c⋅wν′​ for all ν.

Caveat: The constant c depends on the choice of universal Turing machine U, and adversarial choices of U can make AIXI behave arbitrarily badly (Leike & Hutter 2015).

See (Hutter et al. 2024): Chapter 2.7 for Kolmogorov complexity, Chapters 3.7–3.8 for the model class and universal prior, and Chapter 7.4 for AIXI itself.

1. Properties of the Bayesian Mixture

Exercise 1.1 (∗) (Posterior update) [10]. Show that the posterior updates multiplicatively:

w(ν∣æ1:t​) = w(ν∣æ<t​)ξ(et​∣æ<t​at​)ν(et​∣æ<t​at​)​.
Hint

Use the definitions of w(ν∣æ1:t​) and w(ν∣æ<t​), and apply Exercise 0.2.

Solution

From the definition: w(ν∣æ1:t​)=wν​⋅ν(æ1:t​)/ξ(æ1:t​) and w(ν∣æ<t​)=wν​⋅ν(æ<t​)/ξ(æ<t​).

Dividing:

w(ν∣æ<t​)w(ν∣æ1:t​)​=ν(æ<t​)ν(æ1:t​)​⋅ξ(æ1:t​)ξ(æ<t​)​=ξ(et​∣æ<t​at​)ν(et​∣æ<t​at​)​,

where we used the chain rule (Exercise 0.2) for both ν and ξ.

Exercise 1.2 [15]. (One-step predictive distribution of ξ) Starting from ξ(æ1:t​)=∑ν∈M​wν​ν(æ1:t​), derive the one-step predictive form:

ξ(et​∣æ<t​at​) = ν∈M∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)ν(et​∣æ<t​at​).
Hint

Write ξ(et​∣æ<t​at​)=ξ(æ1:t​)/ξ(æ<t​), expand the numerator, and use Exercise 0.2.

Solution

The one-step conditional is the ratio of joint to marginal: ξ(et​∣æ<t​at​):=ξ(æ1:t​)/ξ(æ<t​).

Expanding the numerator using ξ(æ1:t​)=∑ν​wν​ν(æ1:t​):

ξ(et​∣æ<t​at​)    ​= ξ(æ<t​)∑ν∈M​wν​ν(æ1:t​)​= ξ(æ<t​)∑ν​wν​ν(æ<t​)⋅ν(et​∣æ<t​at​)​(chain rule, Exercise 0.2)= ν∑​=w(ν∣æ<t​)ξ(æ<t​)wν​ν(æ<t​)​​​⋅ν(et​∣æ<t​at​)= ν∈M∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)ν(et​∣æ<t​at​).​

Exercise 1.3 (Bounded value) [10]. Show that Vνπ,m​(æ<t​)∈[0,1] for any ν,π,m∈N∪{∞},æ<t​.

Hint

Recall the formula for geometric series: (1−γ)∑k=0n​γk=1−γn+1.

Solution

Since rk​∈[0,1], each discounted reward sum is bounded:

0 ≤ (1−γ)Gt−1:m​ ≤ (1−γ)k=t∑m​γk−t = 1−γm−t+1 ≤ 1.

The interaction measure satisfies νπ(æt:m′​∣æ<t​)≥0 and ∑æt:m′​​νπ(æt:m′​∣æ<t​)=1, so the value function is a weighted average of terms in [0,1]:

0 ≤ Vνπ,m​(æ<t​) = æt:m′​∑​νπ(æt:m′​∣æ<t​)(1−γ)Gt−1:m​ ≤ 1.

For m=∞: since 0≤Vνπ,m​(æ<t​)≤1 for all finite m, the limit Vνπ​(æ<t​)=limm→∞​Vνπ,m​(æ<t​) also lies in [0,1].

Exercise 1.4 (∗) [15]. (Multi-step posterior linearity of ξπ) Extend Exercise 1.2 to multi-step histories: show that for finite m≥t,

ξπ(æt:m​∣æ<t​) = ν∈M∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)νπ(æt:m​∣æ<t​).
Hint

Apply the general chain rule (Exercise 0.5) to ξ(æ1:m​)=∑ν​wν​ν(æ1:m​), then use factorization (Exercise 0.1).

Solution

Start from the definition ξ(æ1:m​)=∑ν∈M​wν​ν(æ1:m​). Apply the general chain rule (Exercise 0.5) to both sides: ξ(æ1:m​)=ξ(æ<t​)⋅ξ(æt:m​∣æ<t​) and ν(æ1:m​)=ν(æ<t​)⋅ν(æt:m​∣æ<t​). Dividing by ξ(æ<t​):

ξ(æt:m​∣æ<t​)  ​= ν∈M∑​ξ(æ<t​)wν​ν(æ<t​)​ν(æt:m​∣æ<t​)= ν∈M∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)ν(æt:m​∣æ<t​).​

Now multiply both sides by π(æt:m​∣æ<t​). By factorization (Exercise 0.1), π(æt:m​∣æ<t​)⋅ξ(æt:m​∣æ<t​)=ξπ(æt:m​∣æ<t​) and likewise for each ν:

ξπ(æt:m​∣æ<t​) = ν∈M∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)νπ(æt:m​∣æ<t​).

2. Existence of Optimal Policies

Recall that Vν∗​(æ<t​):=supπ​Vνπ​(æ<t​) is defined as a supremum over all policies. In general, a supremum need not be achieved: for example, supx∈(0,1)​x=1, but no x∈(0,1) attains this value. This problem shows that in our setting, the supremum is attained, so an optimal policy πν∗​ with Vνπν∗​​=Vν∗​ exists.

Exercise 2.1 [05]. Consider a single time step. Given history æ<t​ and a function Q:A→R, show that supπ​∑a∈A​π(a∣æ<t​)Q(a)=maxa∈A​Q(a), and that the supremum is attained by the deterministic policy that places all probability on an action achieving the maximum.

Solution

Let a∗∈argmaxa′∈A​Q(a′), which exists because A is finite. So Q(a∗)=maxa′​Q(a′).

Upper bound. For any π: ∑a​π(a∣æ<t​)Q(a)≤∑a​π(a∣æ<t​)Q(a∗)=Q(a∗).

Lower bound. The deterministic π∗ with π∗(a∗∣æ<t​)=1 achieves Q(a∗).

Combining: supπ​∑a​π(a)Q(a)=Q(a∗)=maxa′​Q(a′), attained by π∗.

Exercise 2.2 (Bellman equation) [15]. Show that for finite m and t≤m:

Vνπ,m​(æ<t​) = æt′​∑​νπ(æt′​∣æ<t​)[(1−γ)rt′​ + γVνπ,m​(æ<t​æt′​)],
Hint

Use the general chain rule (Exercise 0.5) to peel off the first step,

νπ(æt:m​∣æ<t​) = νπ(æt​∣æ<t​)⋅νπ(æt+1:m​∣æ1:t​).

Break up the sum ∑æt:m​​=∑æt​​∑æt+1:m​​, and factor out rt′​ using ∑æt+1:m′​​νπ(æt+1:m′​∣æ)=1 for any history æ.

Solution

Step 1: Factor the future. Write æt:m′​=æt′​æt+1:m′​: νπ(æt:m′​∣æ<t​)=νπ(æt′​∣æ<t​)⋅νπ(æt+1:m′​∣æ<t​æt′​).

Step 2: Split the reward sum. This is just the return recursion (Definition 0.3): Gt−1:m​=rt′​+γGt:m​, where Gt−1:m​=∑k=tm​γk−trk′​ is the return given æ<t​.

Step 3: Substitute into the definition of Vνπ,m​(æ<t​).

Vνπ,m​(æ<t​) ​= (1−γ)æt′​∑​νπ(æt′​∣æ<t​)æt+1:m′​∑​νπ(æt+1:m′​∣æ<t​æt′​)×[rt′​+γGt:m​].​

Consider the inner term ∑æt+1:m′​​νπ(æt+1:m′​∣æ<t​æt′​)[rt′​+γGt:m​]. We can expand as:

​=æt+1:m′​∑​νπ(æt+1:m′​∣æ<t​æt′​)rt′​+γæt+1:m′​∑​νπ(æt+1:m′​∣æ<t​æt′​)Gt:m​=rt′​æt+1:m′​∑​νπ(æt+1:m′​∣æ<t​æt′​)​+γæt+1:m′​∑​νπ(æt+1:m′​∣æ<t​æt′​)Gt:m​=rt′​+γæt+1:m′​∑​νπ(æt+1:m′​∣æ<t​æt′​)Gt:m​​

as rt′​ doesn't depend on æt+1:m′​, and ∑æt+1:m′​​νπ(æt+1:m′​∣æ<t​æt′​)=1. Inserting this above, we obtain:

Vνπ,m​(æ<t​)​=æt′​∑​νπ(æt′​∣æ<t​)[(1−γ)rt′​+γ=Vνπ,m​(æ<t​æt′​)(1−γ)æt+1:m′​∑​νπ(æt+1:m′​∣æ<t​æt′​)Gt:m​​​].​

Exercise 2.3 (∗) (Backward induction) [20]. Using the Bellman equation from Exercise 2.2 and Exercise 2.1, show by backward induction on t=m,m−1,…,1 that for each finite m, a deterministic optimal policy exists.

Solution

We induct on t=m,m−1,…,1, showing that for every history æ<t​, a deterministic policy achieves Vν∗,m​(æ<t​).

Base case (t=m): At t=m the continuation term vanishes (the value from time m+1 is an empty sum), so the Bellman equation gives Vνπ,m​(æ<m​)=(1−γ)∑æm′​​νπ(æm′​∣æ<m​)rm′​. Splitting the step æm′​=am′​em′​ via νπ(æm′​∣æ<m​)=π(am′​∣æ<m​)ν(em′​∣æ<m​am′​) gives Vνπ,m​(æ<m​)=(1−γ)∑am′​​π(am′​∣æ<m​)∑em′​​ν(em′​∣æ<m​am′​)rm′​. This has the form ∑a​π(a)Q(a) with Q(a)=(1−γ)∑em′​​ν(em′​∣æ<m​a)rm′​, which is independent of π. By Exercise 2.1, the supremum over π is maxa​Q(a), attained by the deterministic policy playing a∗∈argmaxa​Q(a).

Inductive step: Suppose that for every history of length t, there exists a deterministic policy πt+1∗​ achieving Vνπt+1∗​,m​=Vν∗,m​ from time t+1 onwards. Substituting this optimal continuation into the Bellman equation from Exercise 2.2 gives

Vνπ,m​(æ<t​) = æt′​∑​νπ(æt′​∣æ<t​)[(1−γ)rt′​+γVν∗,m​(æ<t​æt′​)].

Splitting the step æt′​=at′​et′​ via νπ(æt′​∣æ<t​)=π(at′​∣æ<t​)ν(et′​∣æ<t​at′​) and grouping the percept sum into the action weight:

Vνπ,m​(æ<t​) = at′​∑​π(at′​∣æ<t​)Q(at′​),

where Q(at′​):=∑et′​​ν(et′​∣æ<t​at′​)[(1−γ)rt′​+γVν∗,m​(æ<t​at′​et′​)] is independent of π (the continuation value Vν∗,m​ is fixed by the inductive hypothesis). By Exercise 2.1, supπ​∑at′​​π(at′​)Q(at′​)=maxat′​​Q(at′​), attained by the deterministic policy playing at∗​∈argmaxat′​​Q(at′​) at time t, then following πt+1∗​.

Exercise 2.4 (Bellman optimality equation) [10]. Using Exercise 2.3, show that for finite m:

Vν∗,m​(æ<t​) = at′​max​et′​∑​ν(et′​∣æ<t​at′​)[(1−γ)rt′​ + γVν∗,m​(æ<t​æt′​)].

where et′​=ot′​rt′​ and æt′​=at′​et′​.

Solution

By Exercise 2.3, a deterministic optimal policy πν∗​ exists with Vνπν∗​,m​=Vν∗,m​. Substituting π=πν∗​ into the Bellman equation from Exercise 2.2 (using Vνπν∗​,m​=Vν∗,m​ on both sides):

Vν∗,m​(æ<t​) = æt′​∑​νπν∗​(æt′​∣æ<t​)[(1−γ)rt′​+γVν∗,m​(æ<t​æt′​)].

Splitting the step æt′​=at′​et′​ via νπν∗​(æt′​∣æ<t​)=πν∗​(at′​∣æ<t​)ν(et′​∣æ<t​at′​):

Vν∗,m​(æ<t​) ​= at′​∑​πν∗​(at′​∣æ<t​)×et′​∑​ν(et′​∣æ<t​at′​)[(1−γ)rt′​+γVν∗,m​(æ<t​at′​et′​)].​

Since πν∗​ is deterministic, let at∗​ denote the unique action with πν∗​(at∗​∣æ<t​)=1. Then:

Vν∗,m​(æ<t​) = et′​∑​ν(et′​∣æ<t​at∗​)[(1−γ)rt′​+γVν∗,m​(æ<t​at∗​et′​)].

Define Q(a):=∑et′​​ν(et′​∣æ<t​a)[(1−γ)rt′​+γVν∗,m​(æ<t​aet′​)]. Then Vν∗,m​(æ<t​)=Q(at∗​). We must have Q(at∗​)=maxa​Q(a): if some a~ had Q(a~)>Q(at∗​), then the policy that plays a~ at æ<t​ and follows πν∗​ elsewhere would achieve value Q(a~)>Vν∗,m​(æ<t​), contradicting Vν∗,m​=supπ​Vνπ,m​. Hence:

Vν∗,m​(æ<t​) = at′​max​et′​∑​ν(et′​∣æ<t​at′​)[(1−γ)rt′​+γVν∗,m​(æ<t​at′​et′​)].

Exercise 2.5 (∗) [15]. (Existence of Vν∗​) Show that the pointwise limit Vν∗​(æ<t​):=limm→∞​Vν∗,m​(æ<t​) exists for all histories æ<t​.

Hint

Show Vν∗,m+1​(æ<t​)≥Vν∗,m​(æ<t​) by expanding Vν∗,m+1​. Use this and Exercise 1.3 and Monotone Convergence Theorem to obtain the result.

Solution

We show Vν∗,m+1​(æ<t​)≥Vν∗,m​(æ<t​) for all æ<t​. Since Vν∗,m+1​=supπ​Vνπ,m+1​, it suffices to show Vνπ,m+1​(æ<t​)≥Vνπ,m​(æ<t​) for every π. Expanding the definition:

    ​Vνπ,m+1​(æ<t​)= (1−γ)æt:m+1​∑​νπ(æt:m+1​∣æ<t​)Gt−1:m+1​= (1−γ)æt:m+1​∑​νπ(æt:m+1​∣æ<t​)[Gt−1:m​ + γm+1−trm+1​]= (1−γ)æt:m+1​∑​νπ(æt:m+1​∣æ<t​)Gt−1:m​+ ≥0(1−γ)γm+1−tæt:m+1​∑​νπ(æt:m+1​∣æ<t​)rm+1​​​.​

For the first term, marginalize over am+1​,em+1​ (which Gt−1:m​ does not depend on):

æt:m+1​∑​νπ(æt:m+1​∣æ<t​)Gt−1:m​ = æt:m​∑​νπ(æt:m​∣æ<t​)Gt−1:m​.

So Vνπ,m+1​(æ<t​)≥(1−γ)∑æt:m​​νπ(æt:m​∣æ<t​)Gt−1:m​=Vνπ,m​(æ<t​).

Since Vν∗,m​(æ<t​) is non-decreasing in m and bounded in [0,1] by Exercise 1.3, the monotone convergence theorem gives that Vν∗​(æ<t​):=limm→∞​Vν∗,m​(æ<t​) exists for each æ<t​.

Exercise 2.6 (Infinite-horizon Bellman optimality equation) [10]. Show that the Bellman optimality equation (Exercise 2.4) extends to m=∞:

Vν∗​(æ<t​) = at′​max​et′​∑​ν(et′​∣æ<t​at′​)[(1−γ)rt′​ + γVν∗​(æ<t​at′​et′​)].
Solution

By Exercise 2.4, for every finite m:

Vν∗,m​(æ<t​) = at′​max​et′​∑​ν(et′​∣æ<t​at′​)[(1−γ)rt′​+γVν∗,m​(æ<t​at′​et′​)].

By Exercise 2.5, each Vν∗,m​(⋅) converges pointwise to Vν∗​(⋅) as m→∞. Since A and E are finite, the max and ∑ are over finitely many convergent terms, so:

Vν∗​(æ<t​) = at′​max​et′​∑​ν(et′​∣æ<t​at′​)[(1−γ)rt′​+γVν∗​(æ<t​at′​et′​)].

Exercise 2.7 (∗) (Optimal policy for infinite horizon) [25]. Show that a deterministic policy πν∗​ exists achieving Vνπν∗​​(æ<t​)=Vν∗​(æ<t​) for all æ<t​.

Approach:

(a) Define πν∗​ as the greedy policy (the argmax action from Exercise 2.6).

(b) Write two Bellman equations: one for Vν∗​, one for Vνπν∗​,m​.

(c) Define ΔVνm​:=Vν∗​−Vνπν∗​,m​ and obtain a recursive equation for it.

(d) Iterate out to the finite horizon, noting Vνπν∗​,m​(æ1:m​)=0 (why?)

(e) Bound the tail, take m→∞.

Solution

Step 1: Define the greedy policy. For each history æ<t​, let

at∗​∈at′​argmax​et′​∑​ν(et′​∣æ<t​at′​)[(1−γ)rt′​+γVν∗​(æ<t​at′​et′​)],

which exists because A is finite. Define the deterministic policy πν∗​(a∣æ<t​):=[[a=at∗​]]. By Exercise 2.6, the infinite-horizon Bellman optimality equation becomes:

Vν∗​(æ<t​) = et′​∑​ν(et′​∣æ<t​at∗​)[(1−γ)rt′​+γVν∗​(æ<t​at∗​et′​)].

Step 2: Error recursion. The Bellman equation (Exercise 2.2) holds for any policy, so for πν∗​ at finite horizon m:

Vνπν∗​,m​(æ<t​) = et′​∑​ν(et′​∣æ<t​at∗​)[(1−γ)rt′​+γVνπν∗​,m​(æ<t​at∗​et′​)].

Subtracting this from the equation in Step 1, the (1−γ)rt′​ terms cancel:

Vν∗​(æ<t​)−Vνπν∗​,m​(æ<t​) ​= γet′​∑​ν(et′​∣æ<t​at∗​)×[Vν∗​(æ<t​at∗​et′​)−Vνπν∗​,m​(æ<t​at∗​et′​)].​

The error at time t is γ times a weighted average of errors at time t+1.

Step 3: Iterate the contraction. Write ΔVνm​(æ<t​):=Vν∗​(æ<t​)−Vνπν∗​,m​(æ<t​)≥0 for the error. Step 2 gives:

ΔVνm​(æ<t​) = γet′​∑​ν(et′​∣æ<t​at∗​)ΔVνm​(æ<t​at∗​et′​).

Applying the same recursion at time t+1 (with greedy action at+1∗​ at history æ<t​at∗​et′​):

ΔVνm​(æ<t​) = γ2et′​∑​ν(et′​∣æ<t​at∗​)et+1′​∑​ν(et+1′​∣æ<t​at∗​et′​at+1∗​)×ΔVνm​(æ<t​at∗​et′​at+1∗​et+1′​).

After m−t+1 iterations, summing over all percept sequences et:m′​:

ΔVνm​(æ<t​) = γm−t+1et:m′​∑​(k=t∏m​ν(ek′​∣æ<k′​ak∗​))ΔVνm​(æ<t​æt:m′​),

where æt:m′​=at∗​et′​⋯am∗​em′​ is the history segment generated by πν∗​. By Exercise 0.4, the product of ν-conditionals is νπν∗​(æt:m′​∣æ<t​). At the boundary, Vνπν∗​,m​(æ<t​æt:m′​)=0 (summing over no rewards past horizon m), so ΔVνm​(æ<t​æt:m′​)=Vν∗​(æ<t​æt:m′​)∈[0,1]. Therefore:

ΔVνm​(æ<t​) = γm−t+1æt:m′​∑​νπν∗​(æt:m′​∣æ<t​)Vν∗​(æ<t​æt:m′​) ≤ γm−t+1.

Step 4: Take m→∞. Since 0≤Vν∗​(æ<t​)−Vνπν∗​,m​(æ<t​)≤γm−t+1→0, we have Vνπν∗​,m​(æ<t​)→Vν∗​(æ<t​), i.e. Vνπν∗​​=Vν∗​.

3. Dominance of the Bayesian Mixture

Exercise 3.1 [03]. Show that ξ(æ<t​)≥wν​⋅ν(æ<t​) for every ν∈M.

Solution

ξ(æ<t​)=∑ν′∈M​wν′​ν′(æ<t​)≥wν​ν(æ<t​).

Exercise 3.2 [10]. Conclude that ξπ(æ1:m​)≥wν​⋅νπ(æ1:m​) for any ν∈M and any policy π.

Solution

By Exercise 0.1: ξπ(æ1:m​)=π(æ1:m​)⋅ξ(æ1:m​)≥π(æ1:m​)⋅wν​ν(æ1:m​)=wν​⋅νπ(æ1:m​).

4. Properties of Vξ​

Exercise 4.1 [15]. Show that for finite m:

Vξπ,m​(æ<t​) = ν∈M∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)Vνπ,m​(æ<t​).
Hint

Use the multi-step posterior linearity of ξπ (Exercise 1.4).

Solution

By Exercise 1.4: ξπ(æt:m​∣æ<t​)=∑ν​w(ν∣æ<t​)νπ(æt:m​∣æ<t​). Multiply both sides by (1−γ)Gt−1:m​ and sum over all æt:m​:

Vξπ,m​(æ<t​)   ​= (1−γ)æt:m​∑​ξπ(æt:m​∣æ<t​)Gt−1:m​= (1−γ)æt:m​∑​[ν∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)νπ(æt:m​∣æ<t​)]Gt−1:m​= ν∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)=Vνπ,m​(æ<t​)(1−γ)æt:m​∑​νπ(æt:m​∣æ<t​)Gt−1:m​​​.​

In the last step we exchanged ∑æt:m​​ and ∑ν​; this is valid because both are sums of non-negative terms (or, for finite m, the sum over æt:m​ is finite). So:

Vξπ,m​(æ<t​) = ν∈M∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)Vνπ,m​(æ<t​).

Fact 4.1 (Dominated convergence for sums). If aν,m​→aν​ as m→∞ for each ν, and ∣aν,m​∣≤bν​ for all m with ∑ν​bν​<∞, then ∑ν​aν,m​→∑ν​aν​. (For finite sums this is trivial.)

Exercise 4.2 (∗) (Infinite-horizon linearity) [17]. Show that the result extends to m=∞:

Vξπ​(æ<t​) = ν∈M∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)Vνπ​(æ<t​).
Hint

Take m→∞ in the finite-horizon result. You will need Fact 4.1 to exchange limit and sum for countably infinite M.

Solution

The left side converges: Vξπ,m​(æ<t​)→Vξπ​(æ<t​) by definition.

For the right side, we need to push limm→∞​ through ∑ν​. If M is finite this is immediate. For countably infinite M, we apply Fact 4.1 (dominated convergence for sums):

  • For each ν: aν,m​:=w(ν∣æ<t​)Vνπ,m​(æ<t​)→w(ν∣æ<t​)Vνπ​(æ<t​) as m→∞ by definition.
  • Domination: ∣aν,m​∣≤w(ν∣æ<t​)⋅1=:bν​ for all m, since Vνπ,m​∈[0,1] (Exercise 1.3).
  • Summability: ∑ν​bν​=∑ν​w(ν∣æ<t​)=1<∞.

So Fact 4.1 gives:

Vξπ​(æ<t​) = m→∞lim​ν∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)Vνπ,m​(æ<t​) = ν∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)Vνπ​(æ<t​).

Exercise 4.1 shows Vξπ​ is linear in ν. The optimal value Vξ∗​ is only convex: a single policy must perform well across all ν∈M simultaneously, rather than being tailored to each ν individually.

Exercise 4.3 (∗) [10]. (Convexity of Vξ∗​) Using Exercise 4.1, show that for finite m:

Vξ∗,m​(æ<t​) ≤ ν∈M∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)Vν∗,m​(æ<t​).
Hint

Apply Exercise 4.1 with π=πξ∗​, the Bayes-optimal policy for ξ.

Solution

By Exercise 2.3, a deterministic Bayes-optimal policy πξ∗​ exists with Vξπξ∗​,m​=Vξ∗,m​. Applying Exercise 4.1 with π=πξ∗​:

Vξ∗,m​(æ<t​) = Vξπξ∗​,m​(æ<t​) = ν∈M∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)Vνπξ∗​,m​(æ<t​).

Since πξ∗​ is optimal for ξ but not necessarily for each individual ν, we have Vνπξ∗​,m​(æ<t​)≤Vν∗,m​(æ<t​) for each ν. Since w(ν∣æ<t​)≥0:

Vξ∗,m​(æ<t​) ≤ ν∈M∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)Vν∗,m​(æ<t​).

Exercise 4.4 (∗) [15]. (Non-linearity of Vξ∗​) Show by example that the inequality in Exercise 4.3 can be strict, i.e. Vξ∗,m​ is not linear in ν.

Hint

Consider M={ν0​,ν1​}: predicting a two-headed coin vs. a two-tailed coin.

Solution

Coin-flip prediction. Let A=O=R={0,1}, M={ν0​,ν1​} with wν0​​=wν1​​=21​, horizon m=1. Environment νi​ always shows outcome i, and the agent is rewarded for a correct prediction:

νi​(et​∣æ<t​at​) : ot​=i,rt​=[[at​=i]].

In νi​ the optimal policy plays at​=i, achieving Vνi​∗,m​=1. In ξ=21​ν0​+21​ν1​ the outcome is a fair coin flip, so no policy predicts better than chance: Vξ∗,m​=21​. Therefore:

ν∑​wν​Vν∗,m​(æ<t​) = 21​⋅1+21​⋅1 = 1 > 21​ = Vξ∗,m​(æ<t​).

5. The Expectimax Form of AIXI

We have specified AIXI only implicitly, as the Bayes-optimal policy πξ∗​ (Definition 0.4). We now unroll this definition into the explicit expectimax expression: an alternating sequence of maximizations over actions and ξ-expectations over percepts.

Exercise 5.1 (Expectimax form of AIXI) [20]. By iterating the finite-horizon Bellman optimality equation (Exercise 2.4), show that

Vξ∗,m​(æ<t​) = (1−γ)at​max​et​∑​ξ(et​∣æ<t​at​)⋯​at+1​max​et+1​∑​ξ(et+1​∣æ<t+1​at+1​)⋯am​max​em​∑​ξ(em​∣æ<m​am​)Gt−1:m​​

and hence, collecting the percept factors with the chain rule (Exercise 0.2) and taking m→∞ (Exercise 2.5 and 2.7), that AIXI selects the action

at​​ = πξ∗​(æ<t​) ∈ at​argmax​m→∞lim​et​∑​at+1​max​et+1​∑​⋯am​max​em​∑​ξ(et:m​∣æ<t​at:m​)Gt−1:m​​
Hint

Prove the first display by backward induction on t from m down to 1, using the finite-horizon Bellman optimality equation (Exercise 2.4) and the return recursion Gt−1:m​=rt​+γGt:m​ (Definition 0.3). At each step the leftover reward term (1−γ)rt​ is constant in the deeper variables; carry it inward using ∑ek​​ξ(ek​∣æ<k​ak​)=1 and c+max(⋅)=max(c+⋅).

Solution

Abbreviate the one-step predictor ξk​:=ξ(ek​∣æ<k​ak​), and write the expectimax operator over steps i,…,j as

i:j∑max​​ := ai​max​ei​∑​ξi​ai+1​max​ei+1​∑​ξi+1​⋯aj​max​ej​∑​ξj​,

the alternating "maximize over the action, average over the percept" chain, with the ξk​ weights built in; the single step is k∑max​​:=maxak​​∑ek​​ξk​. Two facts:

  • (E1) Composition: i:j∑max​​=i∑max​​i+1:j∑max​​, by nesting the definition.
  • (E2) Affine pass-through: for any c∈R and λ≥0 not depending on (ai​,ei​,…,aj​,ej​),
c+λi:j∑max​​X = i:j∑max​​(c+λX),

since each layer has ∑ek​​ξk​=1 (so ∑ek​​ξk​(c+λY)=c+λ∑ek​​ξk​Y) and maxa​(c+λg(a))=c+λmaxa​g(a) for λ≥0.

We prove by backward induction on t=m,m−1,…,1 that

Vξ∗,m​(æ<t​) = (1−γ)t:m∑max​​Gt−1:m​.

Base case t=m. Here Gm−1:m​=rm​ and Vξ∗,m​(æ1:m​)=0 (the return past the horizon is empty, Gm:m​=0). The Bellman optimality equation (Exercise 2.4) for ν=ξ gives

Vξ∗,m​(æ<m​) = am​max​em​∑​ξm​[(1−γ)rm​+γ⋅0] = (1−γ)m:m∑max​​Gm−1:m​.

Inductive step. Assume the claim at time t+1, i.e. Vξ∗,m​(æ1:t​)=(1−γ)t+1:m∑max​​Gt:m​ for every length-t history (recall æ<t+1​=æ1:t​). The Bellman optimality equation (Exercise 2.4) at time t reads

Vξ∗,m​(æ<t​) = t∑max​​[(1−γ)rt​+γVξ∗,m​(æ1:t​)].

Substituting the inductive hypothesis and pulling out (1−γ),

Vξ∗,m​(æ<t​) = (1−γ)t∑max​​[rt​+γt+1:m∑max​​Gt:m​].

As rt​ and γ do not depend on (at+1​,et+1​,…,am​,em​), property (E2) carries them inside the inner operator, and the return recursion Gt−1:m​=rt​+γGt:m​ (Definition 0.3) gives

rt​+γt+1:m∑max​​Gt:m​ =(E2) t+1:m∑max​​(rt​+γGt:m​) = t+1:m∑max​​Gt−1:m​.

Recombining the two operators by (E1),

Vξ∗,m​(æ<t​) = (1−γ)t∑max​​t+1:m∑max​​Gt−1:m​ = (1−γ)t:m∑max​​Gt−1:m​,

which expands back into the max/∑ layers of the first display.

Infinite horizon and the action. Taking m→∞ (Exercise 2.5 and 2.7), Gt−1:m​→G≥t−1​ and the chain extends indefinitely, so Vξ∗​(æ<t​)=(1−γ)t:∞∑max​​G≥t−1​. Collecting the per-step factors by the chain rule (Exercise 0.2, iterated), ∏k=tm​ξk​=ξ(et:m​∣æ<t​at:m​). A Bayes-optimal action maximizes this expression; peeling the outer maxat​​ off as an argmax and dropping the positive constant (1−γ) (which does not move the maximizer) gives the stated action.

On-Policy Value Convergence

The following problems prove the first two main results: on-policy value convergence (Section 7), and that AIXI can't be fooled in deterministic environments (Section 8). The path to the self-optimizing property (advanced stretch goal) resumes at Section 9.

6. Bounding Expectation Differences by Total Variation

Definition 6.1 (Total variation distance). The total variation distance between probability measures P and Q on a countable set Ω is TV[Ω](P,Q):=supS⊆Ω​∣P(S)−Q(S)∣, where P(S):=∑ω∈S​P(ω).

Definition 6.2 (Expectation under P). For a probability measure P on a countable set Ω and a function f:Ω→R, the expectation of f under P is EP​[f]:=∑ω∈Ω​f(ω)P(ω).

The following technical lemma is needed for the on-policy value convergence proof.

Exercise 6.1 (∗) [15]. Let f:Ω→[0,c]. Show that ​EP​[f]−EQ​[f]​≤c⋅TV[Ω](P,Q).

Hint

Define A+={ω∈Ω:P(ω)≥Q(ω)} and decompose the expectation difference as a sum over A+ and its complement A−=Ω∖A+.

Solution

Write out the expectation difference using Definition 6.2:

EP​[f]−EQ​[f] = ω∈Ω∑​f(ω)(P(ω)−Q(ω)).

Define A+:={ω∈Ω:P(ω)≥Q(ω)} and A−:=Ω∖A+, and split the sum:

EP​[f]−EQ​[f] = ω∈A+∑​f(ω)(P(ω)−Q(ω)) + ω∈A−∑​f(ω)(P(ω)−Q(ω)).

Bounding the sum over A+. On A+, P(ω)−Q(ω)≥0 and f(ω)≤c, so:

ω∈A+∑​f(ω)(P(ω)−Q(ω))    ​≤ cω∈A+∑​(P(ω)−Q(ω))= c⋅(P(A+)−Q(A+))≤ c⋅Ssup​∣P(S)−Q(S)∣= c⋅TV[Ω](P,Q).​

Bounding the sum over A−. On A−, P(ω)−Q(ω)<0 and f(ω)≥0, so every term f(ω)(P(ω)−Q(ω))≤0:

ω∈A−∑​f(ω)(P(ω)−Q(ω)) ≤ 0.

Combining. EP​[f]−EQ​[f]≤c⋅TV[Ω](P,Q)+0=c⋅TV[Ω](P,Q).

The other direction. Swapping P and Q: define A~+={ω:Q(ω)≥P(ω)}=A−. The same argument gives EQ​[f]−EP​[f]≤c⋅TV[Ω](Q,P)=c⋅TV[Ω](P,Q).

Therefore ∣EP​[f]−EQ​[f]∣≤c⋅TV[Ω](P,Q).

7. On-Policy Value Convergence of Bayes

The following definitions are needed for the on-policy value convergence theorem.

Definition 7.1 (Probability of events). A finite-length event is a set A⊆(A×E)t of histories of fixed length t. Its probability under νπ is

νπ(A) := æ1:t​∈A∑​νπ(æ1:t​).

An event on infinite histories is any set built from finite-length events by countable unions, intersections, and complements.3 Probabilities of such events are uniquely determined by two properties:

  • Normalization: νπ((A×E)∞)=1.
  • Countable additivity: if A1​,A2​,… are pairwise disjoint events, then νπ(⋃n=1∞​An​)=∑n=1∞​νπ(An​).

From these, all standard rules of probability can be derived (e.g. νπ(A∪B)=νπ(A)+νπ(B)−νπ(A∩B), etc.), though we will not prove them here. Two derived properties we use explicitly:

  • Complement: νπ(Ac)=1−νπ(A).
  • Monotone limits: if A1​⊆A2​⊆⋯, then νπ(⋃n=1∞​An​)=limn→∞​νπ(An​).

Further useful notions:

  • Conditional probability: The probability of event A given observed history æ<t​ is
νπ(A∣æ<t​) := νπ(æ<t​)νπ({æ<t​h:h∈A})​.

Example 7.2 (A fair coin shows 1 infinitely often). Let A=O={0,1}, R={0}, and let ν be a fair coin that ignores the action: ν(ot​=1∣æ<t​at​)=21​ for all æ<t​,at​. Consider the event F:=“ot​=1 for infinitely many t”.

Step 1: Build Fc from finite-prefix events. For each t, the set {ot​=0}:={æ1:t​:ot​=0} is a finite-length event. For each N and T≥N, the set DN,T​:=⋂t=NT​{ot​=0} is also a finite-length event (determined by time T). Define CN​:=⋂t=N∞​{ot​=0} ("all zeros from time N onwards"): this is an infinite-history event, built as a countable intersection of finite-length events. Then Fc=⋃N=1∞​CN​ ("eventually all zeros").

Step 2: Compute νπ(CN​)=0. Since DN,T​⊇DN,T+1​⊇⋯ (adding more constraints), the monotone limit property (for decreasing sets) gives:

νπ(CN​) = T→∞lim​νπ(DN,T​) = T→∞lim​(21​)T−N+1 = 0.

(The probability νπ(DN,T​)=(1/2)T−N+1 is independent of π, since ν ignores actions.)

Step 3: By countable additivity: νπ(Fc)≤∑N=1∞​νπ(CN​)=0, so νπ(F)=1. A fair coin shows 1 infinitely often, almost surely.

As such, Fc (the set of all infinite histories containing only finitely many 1s) is a νπ-measure-zero set. Such histories "exist" as infinite sequences, but occur with probability zero.

Definition 7.3 (Covering4). We say Q covers P if Q is positive everywhere P is: P(A)>0⟹Q(A)>0 for all events A. Equivalently: any event that Q rules out, P also rules out. By Section 3, ξπ covers μπ.

Definition 7.4 (Convergence νπ-almost surely). Let ft​:Ht−1→R be a sequence of functions, where ft​ depends on the history æ<t​ of length t−1. We write ft​(æ<t​)→0 νπ-almost surely (νπ-a.s.) if

νπ({æ1:∞​:ft​(æ<t​)→0})=0.

This set is built from finite-prefix conditions: {ft​→0}=⋃n=1∞​⋂N=1∞​⋃t=N∞​{∣ft​(æ<t​)∣>n1​}, so its probability is well-defined (Definition 7.1).

Example 7.5 (Unpacking "ft​→0"). The set {ft​→0} looks intimidating, but it reads naturally from the inside out:

  • {∣ft​(æ<t​)∣>n1​} is a finite-length event: "at time t, the function is at least n1​ away from zero."
  • ⋃t=N∞​{∣ft​∣>n1​}: "at some time t≥N, ft​ is at least n1​ away from zero."
  • ⋂N=1∞​⋃t=N∞​{∣ft​∣>n1​}: "for every N, there is some t≥N where ft​ is at least n1​ from zero", i.e., ft​ exceeds n1​ infinitely often.
  • ⋃n=1∞​⋂N=1∞​⋃t=N∞​{∣ft​∣>n1​}: "for some n1​>0, ft​ exceeds n1​ infinitely often."

This last condition is exactly {ft​→0}: convergence ft​→0 means that for every ε>0, ∣ft​∣≤ε for all sufficiently large t. Its negation is that some ε>0 is exceeded infinitely often.

Each layer is a countable union or intersection of the previous, so the whole set is a well-defined event on infinite histories.

The Bayesian agent uses the mixture ξ because the true environment μ is unknown. A natural question: does planning with ξ eventually become as good as planning with μ? The following theorem says yes: the value of any fixed policy π, as evaluated by ξ, converges to the value under the true environment μ, along histories that μπ actually generates.5 This tells us that the Bayesian mixture "learns" to predict the true environment's value, on policy.

Theorem 7.6 (On-policy value convergence; (Hutter et al. 2024, Theorem 7.3.1)). For any μ∈M and any policy π: Vξπ​(æ<t​)−Vμπ​(æ<t​)→0 as t→∞, μπ-almost surely. That is, the set of infinite histories along which the value difference does not vanish has μπ-probability zero:

μπ({æ1:∞​:t→∞lim​(Vξπ​(æ<t​)−Vμπ​(æ<t​))=0})=0.

The proof reduces to a finite-horizon TV bound (Exercise 7.1), a covering argument (Exercise 7.2), and the Blackwell–Dubins theorem (Exercise 7.3). The only ingredient we do not prove is Blackwell–Dubins itself, which we state as a given fact.

Exercise 7.1 (Finite-horizon TV bound on value difference) [10]. Using Section 6, show that for finite m:

​Vξπ,m​(æ<t​)−Vμπ,m​(æ<t​)​ ≤ TV[Hm−t+1](ξπ(⋅∣æ<t​),μπ(⋅∣æ<t​)),

where Hm−t+1:=(A×E)m−t+1 is the set of all future history segments æt:m​.

Solution

We want to apply Section 6. Identify:

  • Ω:=Hm−t+1=(A×E)m−t+1, the finite set of future history segments æt:m​.
  • P:=μπ(⋅∣æ<t​) and Q:=ξπ(⋅∣æ<t​), the conditional measures over Ω.
  • f(æt:m​):=(1−γ)Gt−1:m​, which satisfies f∈[0,1] by Exercise 1.3 (so c=1).

Then Vνπ,m​(æ<t​)=∑æt:m​​νπ(æt:m​∣æ<t​)f(æt:m​) is exactly EP​[f] (for ν=μ) or EQ​[f] (for ν=ξ). Applying Section 6:

​Vξπ,m​(æ<t​)−Vμπ,m​(æ<t​)​ = ​EQ​[f]−EP​[f]​ ≤ 1⋅TV[Hm−t+1](P,Q).

Exercise 7.2 (Covering) [05]. Show that ξπ covers μπ (Definition 7.3).

Hint

Use Section 3.

Solution

By Section 3, ξπ(æ1:m​)≥wμ​⋅μπ(æ1:m​) for all histories and all m. So for any event A: μπ(A)>0⟹ξπ(A)≥wμ​⋅μπ(A)>0. Hence ξπ covers μπ.

To complete the proof, we need the TV distance on finite segments to vanish μπ-a.s. as t→∞. This follows from the following deep result, which we state without proof:

Fact 7.7 (Blackwell–Dubins merging of opinions (Blackwell & Dubins 1962)). If Q covers P, then supS​∣P(S∣æ<t​)−Q(S∣æ<t​)∣→0 P-almost surely, where the supremum ranges over all measurable events S (including events on infinite histories).

The proof of Blackwell–Dubins requires the Radon–Nikodym derivative and Levy's martingale convergence theorem: tools from measure theory that are beyond the scope of this sheet. See (Hutter et al. 2024, Chapter 3.9) for discussion.

Exercise 7.3 (On-policy convergence) [15]. Using Fact 7.7, Exercise 7.1 and Exercise 7.2, prove Theorem 7.6.

Solution

Step 1: Finite-horizon bound. By Exercise 7.1, for each finite m:

​Vξπ,m​(æ<t​)−Vμπ,m​(æ<t​)​  ​≤ TV[Hm−t+1](ξπ(⋅∣æ<t​),μπ(⋅∣æ<t​))≤ Ssup​​ξπ(S∣æ<t​)−μπ(S∣æ<t​)​,​

where the second inequality uses that the sup over subsets of Hm−t+1 is at most the sup over all measurable events.

Step 2: Take m→∞. The LHS converges to ∣Vξπ​(æ<t​)−Vμπ​(æ<t​)∣ (by definition of the infinite-horizon value as the pointwise limit). The RHS does not depend on m. Hence

​Vξπ​(æ<t​)−Vμπ​(æ<t​)​ ≤ Ssup​​ξπ(S∣æ<t​)−μπ(S∣æ<t​)​.

Step 3: Take t→∞. By Exercise 7.2, ξπ covers μπ. By Fact 7.7 (Blackwell–Dubins) with P=μπ and Q=ξπ, the RHS tends to 0 as t→∞, μπ-a.s. Therefore

​Vξπ​(æ<t​)−Vμπ​(æ<t​)​ → 0μπ-a.s.

Exercise 7.4 (∗) [40]. Prove Fact 7.7.

Hint

See (Blackwell & Dubins 1962). The proof uses the Radon–Nikodym derivative dP/dQ, Levy's martingale convergence theorem, and the Lebesgue decomposition. No elementary proof is known that avoids graduate-level measure theory.

8. AIXI Cannot Be Fooled in Deterministic Environments

Theorem 8.1 (AIXI cannot act poorly in good environments). If μ∈M is deterministic and Vμ∗​(æ<t​)>ε>0 for all t along the history generated by μ and πξ∗​, then Vξ∗​(æ<t​)≥wμ​ε>0 for all t. (Hutter et al. 2024, Theorem 7.4.10)

Exercise 8.1 [10]. Show that Vξ∗​(æ<t​)≥w(μ∣æ<t​)⋅Vμ∗​(æ<t​).

Hint

Use linearity of Vπ (Exercise 4.2).

Solution

By definition, Vξ∗​(æ<t​)=supπ​Vξπ​(æ<t​)≥Vξπ′​(æ<t​) for any policy π′. By Exercise 4.2 (linearity of Vπ in the environment):

Vξπ′​(æ<t​) = ν∈M∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)Vνπ′​(æ<t​).

Choose π′=πμ∗​, the deterministic optimal policy for μ whose existence is guaranteed by Exercise 2.7:

Vξ∗​(æ<t​) ≥ ν∈M∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)Vνπμ∗​​(æ<t​).

Every term is non-negative (w(ν∣æ<t​)≥0 and Vνπμ∗​​≥0). Dropping all terms except ν=μ:

Vξ∗​(æ<t​) ≥ w(μ∣æ<t​)Vμπμ∗​​(æ<t​) = w(μ∣æ<t​)Vμ∗​(æ<t​).

Exercise 8.2 [15]. Show w(μ∣æ<t​)≥wμ​ when μ is deterministic, and combine with Exercise 8.1 to prove Theorem 8.1.

Solution

From Definition 0.1, the posterior weight is:

w(μ∣æ<t​) = wμ​⋅ξ(æ<t​)μ(æ<t​)​ = wμ​⋅∏k=1t−1​ξ(ek​∣æ<k​ak​)∏k=1t−1​μ(ek​∣æ<k​ak​)​.

Since μ is deterministic, for the history that μ actually generates, μ(ek​∣æ<k​ak​)=1 for each k (the environment produces each percept with certainty). So:

μ(æ<t​) = k=1∏t−1​1 = 1.

Meanwhile, ξ(ek​∣æ<k​ak​)≤1 for each k (it is a probability), so ξ(æ<t​)=∏k=1t−1​ξ(ek​∣æ<k​ak​)≤1.

Therefore w(μ∣æ<t​)=wμ​⋅1/ξ(æ<t​)≥wμ​.

Combining with Exercise 8.1:

Vξ∗​(æ<t​) ≥ w(μ∣æ<t​)⋅Vμ∗​(æ<t​) ≥ wμ​⋅Vμ∗​(æ<t​) > wμ​⋅ε > 0.

Remark. With the Solomonoff prior, wμ​=2−K(μ) may be astronomically small. The result guarantees non-zero value, not near-optimal value.

Sections 9–11: Self-Optimizing Policy (Finite Model Class)

We now prove: if any policy can learn to act optimally, πξ∗​ also learns. We restrict to finite M={ν1​,…,νN​} where each νi​ is a proper probability measure.

9. Likelihood Ratios Are Martingales

The following definition and theorem state the main goal of Sections 9–11.

Definition 9.1 (Self-optimizing). Fix a historic policy π. A policy π~ is self-optimizing for M with respect to π if for every ν∈M: Vν∗​(æ<t​)−Vνπ~​(æ<t​)→0 as t→∞, νπ-almost surely.

The percepts e1:∞​ are sampled from ν; the historic actions a<t​ come from π, which may differ from π~.

Theorem 9.2 (Self-optimizing; (Hutter et al. 2024, Theorem 7.5.2)). Let M be finite and fix a historic policy π. If there exists a π~ self-optimizing for M with respect to π, then πξ∗​ is also self-optimizing for M with respect to π: for any μ∈M, Vμ∗​(æ<t​)−Vμπξ∗​​(æ<t​)→0 μπ-almost surely.

Definition 9.3 (Supermartingale). A sequence of functions Xt​:Ht→R≥0​ (each depending on the history æ1:t​) is a μπ-supermartingale if Eμπ​[Xt​∣æ<t​]≤Xt−1​ for all t; that is,

æt​∑​π(at​∣æ<t​)μ(et​∣æ<t​at​)Xt​(æ1:t​) ≤ Xt−1​(æ<t​).

If equality holds, it is a μπ-martingale.

Intuition. A supermartingale is a quantity whose expected future value, given the present, is no larger than its current value: it cannot "drift upward on average." A martingale is the equality case: expected future value equals current value. The key example is the likelihood ratio Xν,t​(æ1:t​):=ν(æ1:t​)/μ(æ1:t​): how much more (or less) likely the observed history is under ν than under the true environment μ. Under μ, this ratio is a martingale: the true environment does not, on average, favour any alternative ν over itself. Non-negativity plus the (super)martingale structure forces Xν,t​ to converge (by Doob's theorem below), which is the engine behind the self-optimizing proof: it lets us separate environments that remain plausible (Xν,∞​>0) from those that are eventually ruled out (Xν,∞​=0), and handle each case differently in Section 11.

Fact 9.4 (Doob's supermartingale convergence). If (Xt​)t≥0​ is a non-negative μπ-supermartingale, then there exists a function X∞​:H∞→R≥0​ of the infinite history such that Xt​(æ1:t​)→X∞​(æ1:∞​) as t→∞, with X∞​(æ1:∞​)<∞, for μπ-almost every infinite history æ1:∞​. That is:

μπ({æ1:∞​∈(A×E)∞:Xt​(æ1:t​)→X∞​(æ1:∞​)}) = 0.

For each ν∈M, define the likelihood ratio

Xν,t​:Ht→R≥0​,Xν,t​(æ1:t​) := μ(æ1:t​)ν(æ1:t​)​,Xν,0​:=1.

Xν,t​ is a function of the history æ1:t​, not a number: different histories give different values. Throughout this section and the next, any unqualified statement of the form "Xν,t​≥c" or "Xν,t​→Xν,∞​" is shorthand for "Xν,t​(æ1:t​)≥c" or "Xν,t​(æ1:t​)→Xν,∞​(æ1:∞​)" holding μπ-almost surely, i.e. on every infinite history outside a set of μπ-measure zero. We will not track these null sets explicitly; their countable union over all claims is still a μπ-null set.

Exercise 9.1 [15]. Show that Xν,t​ is a μπ-martingale: Eμπ​[Xν,t​∣æ<t​]=Xν,t−1​.

Hint

Write Xν,t​(æ1:t​)=Xν,t−1​(æ<t​)⋅ν(et​∣æ<t​at​)/μ(et​∣æ<t​at​). Sum over at​,et​; μ cancels, leaving ∑et​​ν(et​∣æ<t​at​)=1.

Solution

We need to compute Eμπ​[Xν,t​∣æ<t​]. Conditioning on æ<t​ means at​ and et​ are the random quantities (sampled from π and μ respectively). First, write Xν,t​ pointwise as a function of history in terms of Xν,t−1​:

Xν,t​(æ1:t​)  ​= μ(æ1:t​)ν(æ1:t​)​ = μ(æ<t​)ν(æ<t​)​⋅μ(et​∣æ<t​at​)ν(et​∣æ<t​at​)​= Xν,t−1​(æ<t​)⋅μ(et​∣æ<t​at​)ν(et​∣æ<t​at​)​,​

using the chain rule (Exercise 0.2) for both ν and μ. Now take the conditional expectation. Since Xν,t−1​ depends only on æ<t​, it comes out of the expectation:

Eμπ​[Xν,t​∣æ<t​]   ​= Xν,t−1​⋅Eμπ​[μ(et​∣æ<t​at​)ν(et​∣æ<t​at​)​ ​ æ<t​]= Xν,t−1​at​∈A∑​π(at​∣æ<t​)et​∈E∑​μ(et​∣æ<t​at​)⋅μ(et​∣æ<t​at​)ν(et​∣æ<t​at​)​= Xν,t−1​at​∑​π(at​∣æ<t​)et​∑​ν(et​∣æ<t​at​).​

In the last step, μ(et​∣æ<t​at​) cancels. Since ν is a probability measure, ∑et​​ν(et​∣æ<t​at​)=1 for every æ<t​,at​; and ∑at​​π(at​∣æ<t​)=1. Therefore:

Eμπ​[Xν,t​∣æ<t​] = Xν,t−1​⋅1⋅1 = Xν,t−1​.

Since Xν,t​≥0 (a ratio of non-negative quantities), (Xν,t​)t≥0​ is a non-negative μπ-martingale, in particular, a non-negative μπ-supermartingale.

Exercise 9.2 [05]. Apply Fact 9.4 to conclude Xν,t​→Xν,∞​<∞ μπ-a.s.

Solution

Xν,t​ is a non-negative μπ-supermartingale by Exercise 9.1. By Fact 9.4 (Doob's convergence theorem), Xν,t​ converges μπ-a.s. to a finite limit: Xν,t​→Xν,∞​<∞.

Exercise 9.3 [10]. Define Xξ,t​:=ξ(æ1:t​)/μ(æ1:t​). Show Xξ,t​=∑ν​wν​Xν,t​ and Xξ,t​≥wμ​>0.

Solution

From the definition:

Xξ,t​ := μ(æ1:t​)ξ(æ1:t​)​ = μ(æ1:t​)∑ν​wν​ν(æ1:t​)​ = ν∑​wν​⋅μ(æ1:t​)ν(æ1:t​)​ = ν∑​wν​Xν,t​.

By Section 3: ξ(æ1:t​)≥wμ​⋅μ(æ1:t​), so Xξ,t​=ξ(æ1:t​)/μ(æ1:t​)≥wμ​>0.

Since M is finite, Xξ,t​=∑ν​wν​Xν,t​ is a finite sum of convergent sequences, so Xξ,t​→Xξ,∞​:=∑ν​wν​Xν,∞​<∞ μπ-a.s., with Xξ,∞​≥wμ​>0.

10. Change of Measure

Exercise 10.1 [15]. Let A be a set of finite histories of length m. Show:

νπ[æ1:m​∈A] = Eμπ​[Xν,m​⋅[[æ1:m​∈A]]].
Hint

Use Exercise 0.1 to show νπ/μπ=ν/μ=Xν,m​.

Solution

By Exercise 0.1, νπ(æ1:m′​)=π(æ1:m′​)⋅ν(æ1:m′​) and μπ(æ1:m′​)=π(æ1:m′​)⋅μ(æ1:m′​). For any history æ1:m′​ with μπ(æ1:m′​)>0, the policy factors cancel:

νπ(æ1:m′​)  ​= μπ(æ1:m′​)νπ(æ1:m′​)​⋅μπ(æ1:m′​) = μ(æ1:m′​)ν(æ1:m′​)​⋅μπ(æ1:m′​)= Xν,m​(æ1:m′​)⋅μπ(æ1:m′​).​

For histories with μπ(æ1:m′​)=0: since μπ=π⋅μ, some π(ak​∣æ<k′​)=0, which forces νπ(æ1:m′​)=0 too (the same π-factor appears in νπ=π⋅ν). So both sides are zero.

Summing over æ1:m′​∈A:

νπ[æ1:m​∈A]  ​= æ1:m′​∈A∑​νπ(æ1:m′​) = æ1:m′​∈A∑​Xν,m​(æ1:m′​)⋅μπ(æ1:m′​)= Eμπ​[Xν,m​⋅[[æ1:m​∈A]]].​

Exercise 10.2. (Given.) The identity extends to infinite histories: for any event A⊆(A×E)∞,

νπ[A] = Eμπ​[Xν,∞​⋅[[æ1:∞​∈A]]].

This says that Xν,∞​ plays the role of the Radon–Nikodym derivative dνπ/dμπ on the space of infinite histories. The proof rests on two ingredients beyond the scope of this worksheet:

  • L1 martingale convergence (closed martingale / Levy's upward theorem): since Eμπ​[Xν,t​]=1 for every t, the non-negative μπ-martingale (Xν,t​) is uniformly integrable, so Xν,t​→Xν,∞​ in L1(μπ), not merely μπ-a.s. This lets us pass the t→∞ limit through the expectation.
  • Uniqueness of measure extension (Caratheodory / π–λ theorem): both sides of the identity are finite measures on (A×E)∞; the finite-history identity (Exercise 10.1) shows they agree on all cylinder events A=A0​×(A×E)∞, and cylinders generate the full event σ-algebra, so agreement extends uniquely to every event.

We omit the proof and use this identity freely below.

Exercise 10.3 (Markov inequality for change of measure) [15]. Let E be an event of infinite histories. For any ε>0, show that

μπ[E∩{Xν,∞​≥ε}] ≤ ενπ[E]​.
Hint

On E∩{Xν,∞​≥ε}, Xν,∞​≥ε pointwise. Take μπ-expectations and apply Exercise 10.2.

Solution

Let Eε​:=E∩{Xν,∞​≥ε}. On Eε​, Xν,∞​≥ε, so pointwise

Xν,∞​⋅[[æ1:∞​∈Eε​]] ≥ ε⋅[[æ1:∞​∈Eε​]].

Take μπ-expectations and apply Exercise 10.2:

νπ[Eε​] = Eμπ​[Xν,∞​⋅[[æ1:∞​∈Eε​]]] ≥ ε⋅Eμπ​[[[æ1:∞​∈Eε​]]] = ε⋅μπ[Eε​].

Since Eε​⊆E, νπ[Eε​]≤νπ[E]. Dividing by ε gives μπ[Eε​]≤νπ[E]/ε.

Interpretation. A likelihood ratio of at least ε forces νπ and μπ measures of an event to be comparable: μπ of the event can exceed νπ of it only by the factor 1/ε. In particular, if νπ vanishes on E, so does μπ on the part where the likelihood ratio stays bounded away from zero.

11. Proving the Self-Optimizing Property

Fix a policy π~ that is self-optimizing for M with respect to π (Definition 9.1): its existence is the hypothesis of Theorem 9.2. For each ν∈M, define the suboptimality gap

δν,t​:Ht−1→[0,1],δν,t​(æ<t​) := Vν∗​(æ<t​)−Vνπ~​(æ<t​).

As with Xν,t​, we write δν,t​ without its argument when convenient: "δν,t​→0 μπ-a.s." means δν,t​(æ<t​)→0 on every infinite history outside a μπ-null set, and similarly for "δν,t​≤1" etc.

Exercise 11.1 (Chain of inequalities) [20]. Show:

0 ≤ w(μ∣æ<t​)[Vμ∗​−Vμπξ∗​​] ≤ ν∈M∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)δν,t​.
Hint

Use Vξπξ∗​​≥Vξπ~​ and Exercise 4.2.

Solution

We establish two inequalities and chain them.

First inequality: isolate the μ-term. For each ν∈M, the optimal value is at least the value of any policy: Vν∗​(æ<t​)≥Vνπξ∗​​(æ<t​), so Vν∗​−Vνπξ∗​​≥0. Since the posterior weights w(ν∣æ<t​)≥0, every term in ∑ν​w(ν∣æ<t​)[Vν∗​−Vνπξ∗​​] is non-negative. The μ-term is one such term:

w(μ∣æ<t​)[Vμ∗​−Vμπξ∗​​] ≤ ν∈M∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)[Vν∗​−Vνπξ∗​​].

Second inequality: replace πξ∗​ with π~. By definition of the optimal value, Vξ∗​(æ<t​)≥Vξπ~​(æ<t​). Expanding both sides using infinite-horizon linearity (Exercise 4.2, applied to the fixed policies πξ∗​ and π~):

ν∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)Vνπξ∗​​(æ<t​)  ​= Vξ∗​(æ<t​) ≥ Vξπ~​(æ<t​)= ν∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)Vνπ~​(æ<t​).​

Rearranging: ∑ν​w(ν)[Vν∗​−Vνπξ∗​​]≤∑ν​w(ν)[Vν∗​−Vνπ~​]=∑ν​w(ν)δν,t​.

Chaining:

0 ≤ w(μ∣æ<t​)[Vμ∗​−Vμπξ∗​​] ≤ ν∈M∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)δν,t​.

Exercise 11.2 (Vanishing posterior) [10]. Show: if Xν,∞​=0 then w(ν∣æ<t​)→0 μπ-a.s.

Hint

Show w(ν∣æ<t​)=wν​Xν,t−1​/Xξ,t−1​ and use Exercise 9.3.

Solution

From the posterior weight formula, dividing numerator and denominator by μ(æ<t​):

w(ν∣æ<t​) = wν​⋅ξ(æ<t​)ν(æ<t​)​ = wν​⋅ξ(æ<t​)/μ(æ<t​)ν(æ<t​)/μ(æ<t​)​ = Xξ,t−1​wν​⋅Xν,t−1​​,

where Xν,t−1​ and Xξ,t−1​ are evaluated at the length-(t−1) history æ<t​.

If Xν,∞​=0, then Xν,t−1​→0 μπ-a.s. (Exercise 9.2). Since Xξ,t−1​≥wμ​>0 always (Exercise 9.3), the ratio w(ν∣æ<t​)=wν​Xν,t−1​/Xξ,t−1​→0 μπ-a.s.

Exercise 11.3 (Transferring convergence) [20]. Let F:={æ1:∞​:δν,t​(æ<t​)→0}, the set of infinite histories on which the suboptimality gap fails to vanish. Show that μπ[F∩{Xν,∞​>0}]=0.

Hint

Self-optimizing (Definition 9.1) gives νπ[F]=0. Apply Exercise 10.3 with E=F and ε=1/n to conclude μπ[F∩{Xν,∞​≥1/n}]=0 for each n≥1. Then note {Xν,∞​>0}=⋃n≥1​{Xν,∞​≥1/n} and take the countable union (Definition 7.1).

Solution

Step 1: F is νπ-null. By the self-optimizing assumption (Definition 9.1), under νπ the suboptimality gap δν,t​ vanishes, so νπ[F]=0.

Step 2: Apply Exercise 10.3. For each n≥1, take E=F and ε=1/n:

μπ[F∩{Xν,∞​≥1/n}] ≤ 1/nνπ[F]​ = 0.

Step 3: Countable union. The level sets of Xν,∞​ form a nested increasing family: {Xν,∞​>0}=⋃n≥1​{Xν,∞​≥1/n}. Intersecting with F gives F∩{Xν,∞​>0}=⋃n≥1​(F∩{Xν,∞​≥1/n}), a countable union. By countable subadditivity (Definition 7.1):

μπ[F∩{Xν,∞​>0}] =  ≤ n≥1∑​​μπ[⋃n​F∩{Xν,∞​≥1/n}]μπ[F∩{Xν,∞​≥1/n}] = 0.​

What this says. "δν,t​→0 μπ-a.s. on {Xν,∞​>0}" is shorthand for exactly this event statement: among infinite histories on which the likelihood ratio stays bounded away from zero, all but a μπ-null subset are ones where δν,t​(æ<t​)→0. We do not claim convergence on histories where Xν,∞​=0: that case is handled separately in Exercise 11.2 via the posterior weight.

Exercise 11.4 (Single-term convergence) [10]. Combine Exercise 11.2 and Exercise 11.3 to show w(ν∣æ<t​)δν,t​→0 μπ-a.s.

Solution

Fix ν∈M. We show w(ν∣æ<t​)δν,t​→0 μπ-a.s. by considering two exhaustive cases:

Case 1: Xν,∞​=0. By Exercise 11.2, w(ν∣æ<t​)→0. Since δν,t​∈[0,1] (Exercise 1.3), the product w(ν∣æ<t​)⋅δν,t​≤1⋅w(ν∣æ<t​)→0.

Case 2: Xν,∞​>0. By Exercise 11.3, δν,t​→0. Since w(ν∣æ<t​)≤1 (posterior weights are at most 1), the product w(ν∣æ<t​)⋅δν,t​≤1⋅δν,t​→0.

These two cases cover all infinite histories (μπ-a.s.), so w(ν∣æ<t​)δν,t​→0 μπ-a.s.

Exercise 11.5 (Self-Optimizing Theorem) [15]. Combine Exercise 11.4, Exercise 11.1, Exercise 9.3 to finally prove the main result of Theorem 9.2.

Hint

w(μ∣æ<t​)=wμ​/Xξ,t−1​.

Solution

Since M={ν1​,…,νN​} is finite, we can sum Exercise 11.4 over all ν∈M:

ν∈M∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)δν,t​ ⟶ 0μπ-a.s.

From Exercise 11.1:

0 ≤ w(μ∣æ<t​)[Vμ∗​(æ<t​)−Vμπξ∗​​(æ<t​)] ≤ ν∑​w(ν∣æ<t​)δν,t​ ⟶ 0.

So w(μ∣æ<t​)[Vμ∗​−Vμπξ∗​​]→0 μπ-a.s.

It remains to divide by w(μ∣æ<t​). From Exercise 9.3:

w(μ∣æ<t​) = Xξ,t−1​wμ​​.

Fix an infinite history outside the (single) μπ-null set on which Xξ,t​→Xξ,∞​<∞ fails. Along this history:

  • Xξ,t−1​→Xξ,∞​, a finite positive number (with Xξ,∞​≥wμ​>0 by Exercise 9.3).
  • Hence w(μ∣æ<t​)=wμ​/Xξ,t−1​→wμ​/Xξ,∞​>0, so eventually w(μ∣æ<t​)≥wμ​/(2Xξ,∞​)>0.

Dividing the convergence w(μ∣æ<t​)(Vμ∗​−Vμπξ∗​​)→0 by this positive (per-history) lower bound, and using Vμ∗​−Vμπξ∗​​≥0:

Vμ∗​(æ<t​)−Vμπξ∗​​(æ<t​) ⟶ 0μπ-a.s.

This completes the proof of Theorem 9.2.

Remark. We do not need to know which policy π~ is self-optimizing, or whether it is computable. Mere existence suffices. For countable M, this final step is harder: a countable sum of μπ-a.s.-convergent sequences need not converge μπ-a.s. The general proof uses a "convergence of mixture tails" argument (Hutter 2005, Lem. 5.28).

Further reading

  • Hutter, An Introduction to Universal Artificial Intelligence (2024): Chapter 2.7 (Kolmogorov complexity), Chapters 3.7–3.8 (the model class and universal prior), and Chapter 7.4 (AIXI).
  • Hutter, Universal Artificial Intelligence: Sequential Decisions Based on Algorithmic Probability (Springer, 2005) — the original book-length treatment; Lem. 5.28 handles the countable-M self-optimizing case.
  • Blackwell & Dubins, Merging of Opinions with Increasing Information (Ann. Math. Statist., 1962) — the merging-of-opinions theorem behind on-policy value convergence.
  • Leike & Hutter, Bad Universal Priors and Notions of Optimality (COLT 2015) — adversarial choices of the universal Turing machine can make AIXI behave arbitrarily badly.

A. Worked Example: Bayesian Mixture and Value Function

Setup.

  • Actions: A={H,T} (predict the next coin flip)
  • Observations: O={H,T} (actual coin flip)
  • Rewards: R={0,1}, with rt​=[[at​=ot​]]
  • Model class: M={νHH​,νHT​} (two-headed coin, fair coin)
  • Prior: wνHH​​=wνHT​​=21​

Before any interaction (t=1, æ<1​=ϵ):

ξ(o1​=H∣a1​) ​= 21​⋅1+21​⋅21​ = 43​.​

After observing a head (t=2), the posterior updates:

w(νHH​∣æ1​) ​= 21​⋅3/41​ = 32​,​w(νHT​∣æ1​) ​= 21​⋅3/41/2​ = 31​.​

Updated prediction: ξ(o2​=H∣æ1​a2​)=32​⋅1+31​⋅21​=65​.

Value function. Continuing the same setup, suppose the agent always predicts H (policy πH​).

Under νHH​: always correct, rt​=1 every step: VνHH​πH​​(ϵ)=(1−γ)∑k=0∞​γk⋅1=1.

Under νHT​: correct half the time: VνHT​πH​​(ϵ)=(1−γ)∑k=0∞​γk⋅21​=21​.

The mixture value (by Exercise 4.2) is: VξπH​​(ϵ)=21​⋅1+21​⋅21​=43​.

As the agent observes more heads (μ=νHH​), the posterior on νHH​ increases towards 1, and VξπH​​→VνHH​πH​​=1. This is on-policy value convergence (Theorem 7.6) in action.

B. Knuth's Difficulty Scale

Each subproblem carries a difficulty rating in square brackets, following Knuth's rating scheme for exercises (Knuth 1973) in slightly adapted form. The rating assumes that the material in the preceding problems (on which the subproblem depends) has been understood. In-between values are possible.

[00] Very easy. Solvable from the top of your head.

[10] Easy. Needs 15 minutes to think, possibly pencil and paper.

[20] Average. May take 1–2 hours to answer completely.

[30] Moderately difficult or lengthy. May take several hours to a day.

[40] Quite difficult or lengthy. Often a significant research result.

[50] Open research problem. An obtained solution should be published.

Problems marked (∗) are enrichment: they are off the critical path to the three main results (Theorem 7.6, Theorem 8.1, Theorem 9.2) and can be skipped on a first pass without loss of continuity.
